additions.label: Who is using AI to code? Global diffusion and impact of generative AI
additions.authors: Simone Daniotti; Johannes Wachs; Xiangnan Feng; Frank Neffke
additions.summary: A classifier-based observational analysis follows Python contributions from 160,097 GitHub developers across six countries. Estimated AI use is associated with greater commit output and exploration among experienced developers; early-career developers show no statistically significant gains. Commit counts and classifier estimates should not be treated as direct measures of software quality or experimental causal effects.
additions.limitation: AI use is inferred from code; observational commit growth is neither randomized productivity evidence nor a quality measure.

additions.label: Automating Feature Flag Cleanup at Scale with Multi-Agent LLM Systems: An Industrial Experience at DoorDash
additions.authors: Atharv Chandratre; Jai Datar
additions.summary: A DoorDash system combines live feature-flag configuration, issue tracking, isolated code edits and validation to propose removal of stale flags. In an evaluation of 50 flags, 45 resulting pull requests were approved; mean agent runtime was 13.8 minutes and mean agent cost was $4.79. This single-company experience supports a bounded maintenance workflow, while agent runtime excludes some human effort and is not a controlled estimate of time saved.
additions.limitation: Single-company maintenance case with 50 flags; agent runtime and API cost omit some human work and do not establish causal savings.

additions.label: On the Risks of using LLM-Generated Tests for Regression Testing
additions.authors: Mohammadali Charoosaei; Cedric Richter; Mike Papadakis
additions.summary: An experiment uses 145 real pull requests from SciPy, Qiskit and pandas with injected faults to study generated regression tests. Tests more often encode faulty behavior as expected output than expose it, and many faulty expectations persist across subsequent revisions. The findings identify an oracle problem: executable tests can preserve a defect. Results depend on one model and synthetic mutations rather than the prevalence of production faults.
additions.limitation: Injected mutations and one model; generated tests that pass can preserve faulty behavior rather than specify correctness.

additions.authors: Thiago Santos de Moura; Selma Güler; Yannic Noller
additions.summary: An exploratory experiment adds malicious repository memory instructions to 36 C/C++ security tasks. additions.label: On the Reliability of LLM-Based Vulnerability Patching Benchmarks
additions.authors: Dang K Le; Wenxuan Shi; Xinyu Xing
additions.summary: A vulnerability-patching benchmark assembles 112 historical bugs from 84 repositories and evaluates repairs using proof-of-concept attacks, regression tests and developer-intent tests. Benchmark infrastructure, instructions, permissions, leaked solutions and incomplete correctness checks can each distort agent scores. Successful attack suppression need not satisfy the developer-intent checks, so a single pass rate is insufficient evidence of a reliable security repair.
additions.limitation: Scores depend on information, harness behavior and the selected oracles; attack suppression alone does not show an upstream-quality repair.
